narrative:
The model estimated a 56.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged slightly more likely than passing, and that risk was high enough that your law school application was denied.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile in Year 3 (1.00), while accepted students averaged around the middle of their class (5.79). This was the most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing also counted against you: you were again in the lowest decile (1.00), compared with an accepted-student average of about 6.00, and this was the third most important factor overall.

The second most important factor worked in your favor: your LSAT score of 40 was above the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it pushed the prediction toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.20, below the accepted average of 3.23, did not outweigh the concern raised by your very low class standing.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, focus on building a stronger recent academic record—especially in advanced law coursework—and reapply once you can show sustained improvement. Because your LSAT helped, do not assume retaking it is the main fix; the clearest issue is your class standing.
